title: Die klare Sonne bringts an den Tag
titleEn: The Clear Sun Brings It to Light
part: The Clear Sun Brings It to Light
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 115. Text from Wikisource („Die klare Sonne bringts an den Tag (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 115 tells of a penniless journeyman tailor who meets a Jewish traveller on the road, decides — wrongly — that the man must be carrying money, and beats him to death when the little he actually has, eight heller, turns out not to be worth the trouble; the dying man's last words are, “The clear sun will bring it to light.” Years later, married and settled with children, the tailor is unsettled one morning by sunlight bouncing off his coffee cup and flickering on the wall, and mutters that the sun is trying, and failing, to expose him. His wife presses him until he confesses the old murder and swears her to silence; within three days the whole town knows, and he is brought before the court and executed. The tale closes by noting, without further comment, that the sun got its way after all. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, ward, Armuth and todt.

advisory.lede: This tale turns on a period stereotype — that a Jew must be carrying money — and it contains a murder and an execution.
advisory.more: The tailor kills the Jewish traveller because he assumes a Jew is rich; he finds eight heller. That assumption was a commonplace of the period and is a slander; the 1857 text states it flatly and without comment. The tale's own sympathies, though, are not with the murderer: it says he thrust God out of his heart before he struck, the dying man's words are what the story is named for, and the tailor is tried and put to death. Lectorium presents the text as written.

sentences.t: Ein Schneidergesell reiste in der Welt auf sein Handwerk herum und konnte er einmal keine Arbeit finden, und war die Armuth bei ihm so groß, daß er keinen Heller Zehrgeld hatte.
sentences.l: A tailor’s journeyman travelled about in the world at his trade, and could he once find no work, and was the poverty with him so great that he had not a heller of travelling-money.
sentences.i: A journeyman tailor was travelling about the world at his trade, and one time he could find no work, and his poverty was so great that he had not a heller of travelling money.
sentences.n: A Schneidergesell is a journeyman tailor — a man who has finished his apprenticeship and now travels from master to master looking for work. In und konnte er … und war die Armuth the finite verb stands first in both clauses, an older narrative turn where modern German would say und er konnte … und die Armuth war; the same shape can also be read as a conditional, “and if he could once find no work,” and the tale reads either way. Armuth is the 1857 spelling of Armut. A Heller is the smallest copper coin and Zehrgeld is the money one lives on while travelling, so he had nothing whatever.

sentences.t: In der Zeit begegnete ihm auf dem Weg ein Jude, und da dachte er der hätte viel Geld bei sich und stieß Gott aus seinem Herzen,
sentences.l: In that time there met him on the road a Jew, and then he thought that one had much money on him, and thrust God out of his heart,
sentences.i: At that time a Jew met him on the road, and he thought the man must have a great deal of money on him, and he thrust God out of his heart,
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative — ihm — so the German says “there met to him a Jew.” der hätte is the demonstrative “that one” with the subjunctive of reported thought: the money is what the tailor supposes, not what the tale asserts. The motive is a period stereotype, that a Jew must be carrying money; it is the tale’s own assumption, and the tale is about to show it false. stieß Gott aus seinem Herzen, “thrust God out of his heart,” is the text’s own way of marking what follows as damnable.

sentences.t: gieng auf ihn los, und sprach „gib mir dein Geld, oder ich schlag dich todt.“
sentences.l: went at him, and said “give me your money, or I strike you dead.”
sentences.i: he set upon him and said, “Give me your money, or I will strike you dead.”
sentences.n: auf jemanden losgehen: to go at someone, to attack. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging, todt of tot. schlag is the plain present standing for the future, as German constantly does.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Jude „schenkt mir doch das Leben, Geld hab ich keins und nicht mehr als acht Heller.“
sentences.l: Then said the Jew “grant me my life, money I have none and no more than eight heller.”
sentences.i: Then the Jew said, “Spare my life; money I have none, and no more than eight heller.”
sentences.n: schenkt is the plural imperative: the Jew addresses his attacker with the respectful ihr even under the blow, while the tailor answers him with du. jemandem das Leben schenken is the set phrase for sparing a life, literally to make a present of it. Geld hab ich keins puts the object first for emphasis.

sentences.t: Der Schneider aber sprach „du hast doch Geld, und das soll auch heraus,“ brauchte Gewalt und schlug ihn so lange bis er nah am Tod war.
sentences.l: The tailor, however, said “you do have money, and that shall out too,” used force and beat him so long until he was near death.
sentences.i: But the tailor said, “You have money all the same, and out it shall come,” and he used force and beat him until he was near death.
sentences.n: das soll auch heraus has no verb of motion in it: heraus alone carries “shall come out.” brauchte here is the older use of brauchen for “used, employed” (modern gebrauchte). so lange bis: so long until.

sentences.t: Und wie der Jude nun sterben wollte, sprach er das letzte Wort „die klare Sonne wird es an den Tag bringen!“ und starb damit.
sentences.l: And as the Jew now was about to die, he spoke the last word “the clear sun will bring it to the day!” and died with that.
sentences.i: And as the Jew now lay dying, he spoke his last word, “The clear sun will bring it to light!” and with that he died.
sentences.n: wollte here is not “wanted” but “was on the point of” — sterben wollte. an den Tag bringen is “to bring to the day,” our “bring to light”; the literal keeps the German image, since the sun itself is about to do the bringing. This sentence is the tale’s title and its whole plot.

sentences.t: Der Schneidergesell griff ihm in die Tasche und suchte nach Geld, er fand aber nicht mehr als die acht Heller, wie der Jude gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: The tailor’s journeyman reached him into the pocket and searched for money, but he found no more than the eight heller, as the Jew had said.
sentences.i: The journeyman tailor reached into his pocket and searched for money, but he found no more than the eight heller, just as the Jew had said.
sentences.n: ihm in die Tasche is a dative of the person: German says “reached to him into the pocket” where English uses a possessive, “into his pocket.” The eight Heller are the point of the tale — the money he killed for was never there.

sentences.t: Da packte er ihn auf, trug ihn hinter einen Busch und zog weiter auf sein Handwerk.
sentences.l: Then he packed him up, carried him behind a bush and moved on at his trade.
sentences.i: Then he took him up, carried him behind a bush, and went on his way at his trade.
sentences.n: aufpacken: to load up, take up on one’s back — separable, so the particle auf lands at the end of the clause. auf sein Handwerk ziehen is the journeyman’s phrase for travelling in search of work in his craft. The body is disposed of in half a line.

sentences.t: Wie er nun lange Zeit gereist war, kam er in eine Stadt bei einem Meister in Arbeit,
sentences.l: When he now had travelled a long time, he came in a town into work with a master,
sentences.i: When he had travelled a long while, he came into a town, into work with a master,
sentences.n: wie again means “when,” not “how” — you will meet it in this sense constantly. bei einem Meister in Arbeit kommen: to enter employment with a master craftsman.

sentences.t: der hatte eine schöne Tochter, in die verliebte er sich,
sentences.l: that one had a beautiful daughter, into her he fell in love,
sentences.i: and this master had a beautiful daughter, and he fell in love with her,
sentences.n: der hatte begins the new clause with a demonstrative — “that one had” — where English uses a relative, “who had.” in die is the same demonstrative fronted, “into her,” not a relative. sich verlieben governs in with the accusative: one falls in love “into” a person.

sentences.t: und heirathete sie und lebte in einer guten vergnügten Ehe.
sentences.l: and married her and lived in a good, contented marriage.
sentences.n: heirathete is the 1857 spelling of heiratete. vergnügt is “contented, merry.” The tale gives him years of quiet happiness before the sun catches him.

sentences.t: Über lang, als sie schon zwei Kinder hatten, starben Schwiegervater und Schwiegermutter, und die jungen Leute hatten den Haushalt allein.
sentences.l: Over long, when they already had two children, father-in-law and mother-in-law died, and the young people had the household alone.
sentences.i: After a long while, when they already had two children, the father-in-law and the mother-in-law died, and the young couple had the household to themselves.
sentences.n: über lang is an old adverbial phrase, “after a long time” — compare über kurz oder lang, sooner or later. German leaves out the article before Schwiegervater und Schwiegermutter where English wants one.

sentences.t: Eines Morgens, wie der Mann auf dem Tisch vor dem Fenster saß, brachte ihm die Frau den Kaffee,
sentences.l: One morning, as the man sat on the table before the window, the wife brought him the coffee,
sentences.i: One morning, while the man sat on the table by the window, his wife brought him his coffee,
sentences.n: eines Morgens is the genitive of time, “of a morning,” our “one morning.” A tailor sat cross-legged on his work table, which is why he is on it and not at it. die Frau is “his wife”: German uses the plain article where English wants a possessive.

sentences.t: und als er ihn in die Unterschale ausgegossen hatte und eben trinken wollte da schien die Sonne darauf
sentences.l: and when he had poured it out into the saucer and just wanted to drink, then shone the sun on it
sentences.i: and when he had poured it out into the saucer and was just about to drink, the sun shone on it
sentences.n: die Unterschale is the under-dish, the saucer: coffee was poured into it to cool and drunk from it. da picks up the long when-clause and throws the verb schien in front of its subject. The 1857 text sets no comma before da.

sentences.t: und der Widerschein blinkte oben an der Wand so hin und her und machte Kringel daran.
sentences.l: and the reflection flashed up on the wall so to and fro and made rings on it.
sentences.i: and the reflection flickered to and fro high on the wall and made rings there.
sentences.n: der Widerschein is the reflected light thrown back. hin und her, “there and back,” is our “to and fro.” Kringel are little rings or curls — of light here, of dough elsewhere; daran, “on it,” points back to the wall.

sentences.t: Da sah der Schneider hinauf und sprach „ja, die wills gern an den Tag bringen und kanns nicht!“
sentences.l: Then the tailor looked up and said “yes, she would like to bring it to the day and cannot!”
sentences.i: Then the tailor looked up and said, “Yes, she would gladly bring it to light, and cannot!”
sentences.n: die is the sun, feminine in German, so “she” — which keeps the tailor talking to the sun as to a person. wills and kanns are will es and kann es run together, as speech does. gern with a verb means “would like to.”

sentences.t: Die Frau sprach „ei, lieber Mann, was ist denn das? was meinst du damit?“
sentences.l: The wife said “eh, dear husband, what is that then? what do you mean by that?”
sentences.i: His wife said, “Why, dear husband, what is this? What do you mean by it?”
sentences.n: Mann here is “husband,” as Frau above is “wife.” denn in a question is untranslatable filler, roughly “then, tell me.” ei is a mild cry of surprise.

sentences.t: Er antwortete „das darf ich dir nicht sagen.“
sentences.l: He answered “that I may not tell you.”
sentences.n: darf nicht is “may not, dare not” — he is forbidden, not unable. dir is the dative of the person told.

sentences.t: Sie aber sprach „wenn du mich lieb hast, mußt du mirs sagen“
sentences.l: But she said “if you have me dear, you must tell it me”
sentences.i: But she said, “If you love me, you must tell me”
sentences.n: jemanden lieb haben, “to hold someone dear,” is the ordinary German for loving. mirs is mir es run together, the dative before the accusative. mußt is the 1857 spelling of musst.

sentences.t: und gab ihm die allerbesten Worte, es sollts kein Mensch wieder erfahren, und ließ ihm keine Ruhe.
sentences.l: and gave him the very best words, no person should learn it again, and left him no rest.
sentences.i: and she coaxed him with the fairest words — no soul should ever hear of it — and left him no peace.
sentences.n: jemandem gute Worte geben is a set phrase: to coax, to talk someone round. sollts is sollt es; kein Mensch is “nobody”; wieder here is “in turn,” that is, nobody was to hear it from her. The middle clause slips into reported speech with no verb of saying to introduce it, which German does easily and English cannot.

sentences.t: Da erzählte er, vor langen Jahren, wie er auf der Wanderschaft ganz abgerissen und ohne Geld gewesen,
sentences.l: Then he told, long years ago, how he on the journeying had been quite ragged and without money,
sentences.i: Then he told her how, long years before, on the road, he had been quite ragged and without money,
sentences.n: die Wanderschaft is the journeyman’s years of travel from town to town. abgerissen, “torn off,” means ragged, in rags. From here the whole telling stands in the subjunctive of reported speech, which marks it as his words rather than the narrator’s; the auxiliary sei is simply left out.

sentences.t: habe er einen Juden erschlagen, und der Jude habe in der letzten Todesangst die Worte gesprochen „die klare Sonne wirds an den Tag bringen!“
sentences.l: he had struck a Jew dead, and the Jew had in the last agony of death spoken the words “the clear sun will bring it to the day!”
sentences.i: he had struck a Jew dead, and the Jew in his last agony of death had spoken the words, “The clear sun will bring it to light!”
sentences.n: habe … erschlagen and habe … gesprochen are the subjunctive of reported speech: these are the tailor’s words to his wife. die Todesangst is the fear or agony of death. wirds is wird es.

sentences.t: Nun hätts die Sonne eben gern an den Tag bringen wollen, und hätt an der Wand geblinkt und Kringel gemacht, sie hätts aber nicht gekonnt.
sentences.l: Now the sun had just wanted to bring it to the day, and had flashed on the wall and made rings, but it had not been able to.
sentences.i: Now the sun had been wanting to bring it to light, and had flickered on the wall and made rings, but it had not been able to.
sentences.n: Still his reported speech: hätts and hätt are hätte es and hätte, subjunctive. bringen wollen is the double infinitive German uses in place of a past participle after a modal; gekonnt at the end is the participle of können standing alone, with the infinitive understood.

sentences.t: Danach bat er sie noch besonders, sie dürfte es niemand sagen, sonst käm er um sein Leben, das versprach sie auch.
sentences.l: Afterwards he begged her especially, she might tell it to nobody, otherwise he would lose his life, that she promised too.
sentences.i: Afterwards he begged her expressly that she should tell it to no one, or he would lose his life; and she promised.
sentences.n: ums Leben kommen, literally “to come about one’s life,” is to lose it; English cannot keep the German shape, so the literal says “lose.” dürfte and käm are again the subjunctive of reported speech. besonders here is “particularly, expressly.”

sentences.t: Als er sich aber zur Arbeit gesetzt hatte, gieng sie zu ihrer Gevatterin und vertraute ihr die Geschichte, sie dürfte sie aber keinem Menschen wieder sagen;
sentences.l: But when he had set himself to work, she went to her godmother and confided the story to her, but she might tell it to no person again;
sentences.i: But when he had sat down to his work, she went to her godmother and confided the story to her — only she was to tell it to nobody;
sentences.n: die Gevatterin is the woman who stood godmother to a child of the house, a close friend of the family. The whole ruin turns on this one visit: the wife binds her to silence in exactly the words her husband used to bind her.

sentences.t: ehe aber drei Tage vergiengen, wußte es die ganze Stadt, und der Schneider kam vor das Gericht und ward gerichtet.
sentences.l: but before three days passed, the whole town knew it, and the tailor came before the court and was judged.
sentences.i: but before three days were out the whole town knew it, and the tailor was brought before the court and sentenced.
sentences.n: vergiengen is the 1857 spelling of vergingen. ward is the old past of werden, forming the passive. gerichtet werden is to be tried and sentenced — and for murder the sentence was death; the tale states it in four words and moves on.

sentences.t: Da brachte es doch die klare Sonne an den Tag.
sentences.l: Then the clear sun did bring it to the day after all.
sentences.i: So the clear sun brought it to light after all.
sentences.n: doch is the small word carrying the whole ending: “after all, in spite of everything.” The line closes the ring with the dying man’s words, and it is worth saying plainly where the tale’s own sympathy lies: with the murdered man, whose word stands, against the murderer, who hangs.

glossary.hab: haben — have (1st sg. present, short form of habe)
glossary.heller: der Heller — heller, a small copper coin of the least value
glossary.los: losgehen — at, against (separable particle: auf jemanden losgehen, to go at someone — not los, “rid of”)
glossary.packte: packen — took up, hoisted (3rd sg. past; packte auf, from aufpacken: to load up on one’s back)
glossary.schlag: schlagen — strike (1st sg. present; ich schlag dich todt: I strike you dead)
glossary.stieß: stoßen — thrust, shoved (3rd sg. past; Gott aus seinem Herzen stoßen: to thrust God out of one’s heart)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (the noun; not the adverb weg, “away”)
glossary.zog: ziehen — went, travelled (3rd sg. past; zog weiter: went on his way)
